rv.q: A musical-theater performance of genuine perfection
When it comes to this particular couple, Urie and Foster make you believe in a happy future that may include all kinds of calisthenics.
Naturally, Foster makes a banquet of the material, from Winnifred’s entrance, covered in leeches, to her bravura numbers, “Shy” and “After.”
Her performance as Winnifred is the highlight, marked by memorable antics ranging from stuffing an exorbitant number of grapes in her mouth to a delightfully disturbing series of hip thrusts.

In short, Foster nails this performance, bringing what is, ever has been and always will be a mid-tier musical that has more unnecessary subplots and sing-song padding than an old mattress has feathers.
Mary Rodgers’ musical has found Sutton Foster.
She’s clearly having a good time and you either jump on the Good Ship Sutton, or you’ll keep falling overboard all night long.
And the show finally cannot overcome the casting of Foster, a game and fantastic performer who simply can’t find her way into a character who’s all sloppy id.
Director Lear deBessonet gives Sutton Foster the role of a lifetime and the star twinkles ever more brightly as she demonstrate the huge range of her her talent.
The new Broadway revival of Once Upon a Mattress, starring Sutton Foster, stacks up to two hours of pure theatrical fun.
It’s Urie who convinces, for the first time, that this musical isn’t just about a spunky, scrappy princess succeeding against the odds but also a real love story between two moonstruck misfits.
At the Hudson, they're throwing a party, and everyone is having a ball.

Firing on all cylinders, Foster is a tour de force as she sings, dances, performs keg stands, fights raccoons, pulls a ukelele out of her pants, and almost never stops gyrating her hips throughout the musical's two-hour plus runtime.
This is the exemplary first theatrical experience for that young person in your life and a great time spent with joy and laughter for you.
Amidst a sea of comedic talents, she stands first among equals, and my jaw is still aching from smiling.

Once Upon a Mattress offers laughs galore; flights of melody highlighted by the light-hearted romantic ballad “In a Little While,” that upbeat paean to “Normandy,” and that clarion-blasted swamp-heroine’s lament, “Shy”; and is likely to leave a wide grin on the face of happy playgoers.
Long-time fans of the show and newcomers alike will find this production of Once Upon a Mattress a perfect summertime treat.
Foster reminds us of the thrilling spectacle of seeing performers work their magic live.
Mattress is an exceedingly silly show.
Once Upon a Mattress suffers vastly by comparison.
But even if Sutton Foster could replicate Burnett’s star-making performance, the show would still seem dated on the Broadway stage of 2024.
As Princess Fred, Foster is such a pro she pulls it off.
Sutton Foster’s portrayal of Princess Winnifred is the stuff of Broadway legend.
This is just good, old-fashioned fun.
The production was elaborate and witty, and it took no effort to understand and enjoy.
Bottom line, even with its shortcomings it is a highlight of the season so far, just to see the talented Sutton Foster pass the test and prove that she is certainly Broadway nobility!

cn.t: Critics praise Sutton Foster's dazzling comedic performance in this jovial Broadway revival, though some find the old-fashioned material thin. Foster's physical comedy draws raves, but the show itself receives more mixed reactions.

sg.ra: SeatPlan, TickPick and Headout all converge: center rows D-K sit at a perfect distance to take in the whole stage without craning. Row A is called out as too close for comfortable viewing. Dress Circle overhangs at Orchestra row L and the Mezz overhang only becomes obvious at row R without significantly cutting the stage, so the middle band is protected. 2017 ATG restoration upgraded legroom throughout.

SeatPlan flags Dress Circle A-B center as offering unobstructed sightlines and the 'front few rows of the Center Dress Circle' as premium; rows D-F center are repeatedly called out as great-value seats with full sweep of the stage. The 258-seat section has a good rake and generous legroom. Balcony overhang only becomes obvious at row J and doesn't cut into the stage, so every row is usable.

SeatPlan describes Balcony rows A-B center as hanging close enough for detailed views and reports sightlines 'better than average' for a third level. Rear rows G-H are the cheapest in the house. Rake is very good, but legroom is tighter than the rest of the theater and the top of the stage may be cut by the balcony's angle. AVFMS user at G110 noted that some in-audience action isn't visible from rear balcony.
